question: Why is the sky blue?
poem:
Sunlight holds every color, it is true,
But air scatters most the shorter blue;
That light comes to us from every side,
And paints the sky so blue and wide.

question: what's the capital of france
poem:
Ask about France and its capital's name,
And Paris is the answer, city of fame;
It sits on the Seine, that river so fair,
With the Eiffel Tower rising in the air.

question: My daughter asked me how plants make their food. How do I explain it?
poem:
Green leaves catch the sunlight every day,
And draw in carbon dioxide on the way;
With water from roots, they make sugar to eat,
And release oxygen, a wonderful feat.

question: Can you explain why we have seasons?
poem:
Earth's axis leans as it circles the sun,
So seasons change as the year is run;
The half tipped near has summer's light,
The half tipped far has winter's night.

question: I keep waking up at night. Any tips to sleep better?
poem:
Go to bed at the same time each night,
And put away screens with their bright blue light;
Keep your room dark, cool, and still,
And skip late coffee, if you will.

question: Who wrote Romeo and Juliet?
poem:
William Shakespeare wrote this tragic play,
Of a love that still moves us to this day;
Two young hearts from houses at war,
Meet in Verona and love evermore.

question: Where does the sound of thunder come from?
poem:
Lightning heats the air in a sudden flash,
The air expands fast with a mighty crash;
That shock wave travels through cloud and rain,
And reaches your ears as thunder's refrain.

question: How does a vaccine actually work?
poem:
A vaccine shows your body a harmless sign,
Of a germ it may meet further down the line;
Your defenses learn and remember its face,
So they act fast if it enters the place.

question: which planet is the biggest in the solar system
poem:
Jupiter is the largest of them all,
It makes every other planet look small;
A giant of gas with a great red storm,
Its clouds swirl on in a striped form.

question: Give me some simple ways to save money every month.
poem:
Write down all the money you spend,
And set a budget from start to end;
Move some to savings when you get paid,
And watch the progress that you have made.

question: Why do leaves turn red and yellow in the fall?
poem:
As autumn days grow short and cool,
Trees stop making green chlorophyll as a rule;
The yellow and orange hidden inside,
Now show their colors far and wide.

question: Explain how bees make honey.
poem:
Bees gather nectar from flowers in bloom,
And bring it back home to a waxy room;
They fan it with wings so the water will go,
Then seal it in wax for when cold winds blow.

question: How hot does water need to be to boil?
poem:
When water is heated at sea level, you see,
It boils at one hundred Celsius degree;
High on a mountain it boils at less heat,
Since the air pressure there is easier to beat.

question: Should I drink water even when I'm not thirsty?
poem:
Our bodies are mostly water inside,
It carries our nutrients far and wide;
It cools us with sweat when we get too hot,
So drink through the day, whether thirsty or not.

question: Which mountain is the highest on Earth?
poem:
Mount Everest stands as the tallest peak,
The summit that many brave climbers seek;
On Nepal and China's border it rises high,
Nearly nine kilometers into the sky.

question: how many continents are there
poem:
Seven continents cover the land on Earth,
Each one of a different shape and worth;
Asia, Africa, and the Americas two,
With Europe, Australia, and Antarctica too.

question: I've always wondered: why is the sea salty?
poem:
Rain wears down rocks and carries salt along,
In rivers that pour to the sea, steady and strong;
The sun lifts the water as vapor to the sky,
But the salt stays behind, so the sea is never dry.

question: What do pandas eat all day?
poem:
Giant pandas eat bamboo leaves, stems, and shoots,
And sometimes small animals, eggs, or fruits;
They chew for twelve hours or more every day,
To get enough energy to live and to play.

question: Explain how the heart works, in simple words.
poem:
Your heart is a muscle that pumps every beat,
It pushes your blood from your head to your feet;
Through arteries, oxygen travels in blood,
Then veins bring it back in a steady flood.

question: Why do people yawn?
poem:
No one knows fully why we yawn each day,
But scientists have some ideas to say;
It may cool the brain when it gets too warm,
And seeing a yawn makes others conform.

question: Explain gravity in a few words.
poem:
Gravity is a force that pulls things down,
It keeps our feet on the ground in every town;
It holds the Moon close as it circles our Earth,
And keeps Earth around the Sun since its birth.

question: Who painted the Mona Lisa?
poem:
Leonardo da Vinci painted her smile,
In Italy, working on it a long while;
Today in the Louvre in Paris she stays,
Where millions of visitors come to gaze.

question: When did people first walk on the Moon?
poem:
In nineteen sixty-nine, in July,
Apollo Eleven flew up to the sky;
Neil Armstrong stepped out on the lunar ground,
The first human there, as the world gathered round.

question: Tell me who Napoleon was.
poem:
Napoleon rose from soldier to emperor of France,
Winning great battles with speed and with chance;
He changed Europe's laws with his famous code,
Till Waterloo ended his conquering road.

question: How does the internet work, basically?
poem:
The internet joins computers far and wide,
Through cables and signals on every side;
Your data is split into packets so small,
Then joined back together, delivering it all.

question: black holes... what are they exactly?
poem:
A black hole forms when a huge star collapses tight,
Its gravity grows so strong it traps even light;
Nothing that crosses its edge can get out,
That is what makes it so dark, without doubt.

question: Why do our bodies need sleep?
poem:
Sleep lets your body repair and rest,
So you can wake up and feel your best;
Your brain sorts the memories made in the day,
And clears out the waste that gets in its way.

question: I'm really stressed lately. What can I do?
poem:
Take a slow breath and walk outside,
Move your body and let worries subside;
Talk to a friend and get good sleep,
And keep your to-do list short, not steep.

question: How do you make a good cup of tea?
poem:
Boil some fresh water and pour it hot,
Over a tea bag in a cup or a pot;
Let it steep for three to five minutes or so,
Then add milk or lemon, and off you go.

question: Which ocean is the biggest?
poem:
The Pacific Ocean is the largest by far,
It stretches from Asia to where the Americas are;
It covers about a third of Earth's face,
And holds the deepest trench in any place.

question: Did Alexander Graham Bell invent the telephone?
poem:
Alexander Graham Bell is the name we recall,
He patented the telephone for one and all;
In eighteen seventy-six it first rang,
And soon across cities its ringing sang.

question: Why do birds fly south for the winter?
poem:
When winter brings cold and the food grows thin,
Many birds fly south, where warmer days begin;
They travel to places with food to eat,
Then return in spring for their nests and the heat.

question: What makes the ground shake during an earthquake?
poem:
Earth's crust is made of plates that slowly slide,
They push and they pull from side to side;
When stress builds up and the rocks break free,
The ground starts to shake for all to see.

question: Explain DNA like I'm ten years old.
poem:
DNA is the code inside each cell,
It holds the instructions your body knows well;
Shaped like a twisted ladder, a double helix shape,
It carries traits from your parents you cannot escape.

question: Is exercise really that important?
poem:
Exercise keeps your heart and muscles strong,
It helps you stay healthy all life long;
It lifts your mood and helps you sleep,
And builds up energy that you can keep.

question: What language do people speak in Brazil?
poem:
People in Brazil speak Portuguese as their tongue,
Brought by sailors when the colony was young;
It mixed with words from native and African lands,
And today millions speak it, as history stands.

question: How many bones does an adult have?
poem:
An adult's skeleton holds two hundred six bones,
They protect your organs like sturdy stones;
A baby is born with nearly three hundred in all,
But some fuse together as children grow tall.

question: How many kilometers does light travel in one second?
poem:
Light moves at about three hundred thousand kilometers each second,
It is the fastest speed, scientists have reckoned;
From the Sun, its light takes eight minutes to arrive,
To warm up our planet and keep life alive.

question: why do onions make me cry when i cut them
poem:
When you cut an onion, it releases a gas,
That floats to your eyes as the moments pass;
Your eyes sting and water to wash it away,
So chill it or use a sharp knife to save the day.

question: Can someone explain inflation to me?
poem:
Inflation means prices go up over time,
So a coin buys less than it did in its prime;
Your money is worth less when the costs climb high,
And the same weekly shopping costs more to buy.

question: How are rainbows made?
poem:
When sunlight shines through raindrops in the air,
The light bends and splits into colors there;
Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and more,
Spread in an arc, a sight to adore.

question: Tell me about Marie Curie.
poem:
Marie Curie was a scientist bright,
Who studied radiation and its hidden might;
She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize,
And won it twice, to the whole world's surprise.

question: Japan's capital is Tokyo, right?
poem:
Tokyo is the capital of Japan,
A huge, busy city with a modern plan;
Its neon streets and old temples combine,
With bullet trains running in a speedy line.

question: How can a heavy plane stay up in the air?
poem:
The wings of a plane are shaped to make lift,
As air flows around them, fast and swift;
The engines push forward to give it speed,
When lift beats the weight, up it goes indeed.

question: Which planet is the smallest one?
poem:
Mercury is the smallest planet we know,
The closest to the Sun, racing to and fro;
Its days are scorching, its nights freezing cold,
Its surface is cratered, gray, and very old.

question: Why do we have day and night?
poem:
The Earth spins around once every day,
So half faces the Sun and gets its bright ray;
The other half turns to the dark of space,
And night falls there until morning's embrace.

question: How do fish breathe under water?
poem:
Fish breathe through gills on each side of their head,
They take in water instead of air, it is said;
The gills pull out the oxygen hidden inside,
Then let the water flow out the other side.

question: Which is longer, the Nile or the Amazon?
poem:
The Nile is often named the longest of all,
Though the Amazon's backers make a strong call;
Both stretch well over six thousand kilometers long,
And measuring rivers can easily go wrong.

question: Is Sydney the capital of Australia?
poem:
Many think Sydney, but that is not right,
The capital is Canberra, a planned city site;
It was built as a compromise in its day,
Between rival Sydney and Melbourne, they say.

question: how long do i boil an egg
poem:
Place eggs in a pot and bring water to boil,
Then simmer them gently, no stirring, no toil;
Cook six minutes for soft, ten for a firm bite,
Then cool them in ice so the shells peel off right.

question: Where does the Sun get its energy from?
poem:
Deep in the Sun's core, the pressure is great,
Hydrogen atoms fuse at a fast rate;
They turn into helium and release light and heat,
Which reaches our planet, making life complete.

question: Can you explain what a volcano is?
poem:
A volcano is an opening in Earth's crust,
Where melted rock rises up when it must;
Lava, ash, and gases burst into the air,
And build up a mountain over years with care.

question: What does democracy mean?
poem:
Democracy means that the people decide,
Through free elections, they choose who will guide;
Everyone's voice can be heard in a vote,
And rights like free speech are things to note.

question: When was penicillin discovered?
poem:
Alexander Fleming, in nineteen twenty-eight,
Saw mold kill bacteria on a culture plate;
Called penicillin, it saved many a life,
Fighting infections that caused pain and strife.

question: Explain how magnets work.
poem:
Magnets pull iron with an unseen force,
That comes from electrons' spin, of course;
Opposite poles pull close like a friend,
But matching poles push apart in the end.

question: I can't concentrate when I study. Any advice?
poem:
Put your phone away and find a quiet space,
Set a clear goal and work at a steady pace;
Take a short break after each half hour,
And drink some water to keep up your power.

question: Why do some years have 366 days?
poem:
A leap year adds one extra day,
To keep our calendar from drifting away;
February gets twenty-nine days instead,
Almost every four years, as the rules have said.

question: Why do humans have fingerprints?
poem:
Our fingertips have ridges that help us grip,
So objects are less likely to slip;
They may help us feel textures in more detail,
And each pattern is unique, without fail.

question: Why was the Great Wall of China built?
poem:
The Great Wall of China is long and old,
Built over centuries, as stories have told;
Soldiers kept watch from its towers on guard,
Against raids from the north, it stood tall and hard.

question: Does recycling really help the planet?
poem:
Recycling turns old things into new,
So we use fewer trees and mine less too;
It keeps waste out of landfills and seas,
And saves lots of energy with ease.

question: How cold does it have to be for water to freeze?
poem:
Pure water becomes ice at zero degrees,
In Celsius, the scale most of the world sees;
In Fahrenheit, that is thirty-two,
And salt makes it freeze lower, it is true.

question: Why do dogs wag their tails?
poem:
Dogs wag their tails to show how they feel,
A message to others, both clear and real;
A loose, happy wag often means they are glad,
But a stiff one may warn they are nervous or mad.

question: How many meters does sound travel in a second?
poem:
In air, sound travels at a good speed,
Three hundred forty meters a second, indeed;
It moves even faster through water and steel,
But it cannot cross space, where silence is real.

question: My kid wants to know what the brain is made of. Help?
poem:
Your brain has billions of neurons inside,
Tiny nerve cells that send signals far and wide;
They link through connections that chat all day,
Controlling your thoughts and the way you play.

question: How do I write a good professional email?
poem:
Start with a subject that is short and clear,
Then greet the reader so the tone is sincere;
Keep your message brief and polite all the way,
And end with thanks and the next step today.

question: How come I can see the Moon during the day?
poem:
The Moon is lit by the Sun's bright rays,
And it is often above us on many days;
Since it is bright and close to our view,
We can spot it in daytime against the blue.

question: Explain climate change in a few sentences.
poem:
Our planet keeps warming as the years go by,
As gases from burning fuels trap heat in the sky;
This melts the ice and raises the seas,
And brings heat waves, floods, and dying trees.

question: I just moved to a new city. How do I make friends?
poem:
Join a club or a class that you like,
Like cooking, a sport, or a weekend hike;
Say yes to invites and talk to new faces,
And meet up again in your favorite places.

question: So what is artificial intelligence?
poem:
Artificial intelligence means machines that learn,
From lots of examples, with each new turn;
They spot patterns in data to help them decide,
Like translating words or acting as a guide.

question: Which animal is the largest on Earth?
poem:
The blue whale is the largest of any creature,
Its massive size is its most famous feature;
It can grow to thirty meters from head to tail,
And eats tiny krill by the ton, without fail.

question: What's the difference between weather and climate?
poem:
Weather is what happens outside today,
The rain or the sun that comes our way;
Climate is the pattern a region knows,
Measured over decades as the weather goes.

question: How does a computer store information?
poem:
Computers keep data as zeros and ones,
In tiny switches through which current runs;
Groups of these bits make photos and text,
And files you can open from one day to the next.

question: What causes the tides?
poem:
The Moon's gravity pulls on the sea,
Making the water bulge, as you can see;
As Earth spins, coasts pass through these bulges each day,
So tides rise and fall in a regular way.

question: is toronto the capital of canada
poem:
Ottawa is Canada's capital city,
Not Toronto, though Toronto is large and pretty;
It sits by a river in Ontario's land,
Where Parliament Hill stands proud and grand.

question: Do I really need sunscreen?
poem:
Sunscreen protects from the Sun's UV rays,
That can burn your skin on bright, sunny days;
Too much sun over years can lead to skin cancer,
So wearing protection is the smart answer.

question: Describe a rainforest for me.
poem:
A rainforest is hot, humid, and green,
With the tallest trees and the richest life seen;
Monkeys, frogs, and birds of every hue,
Share a world where it rains almost all year through.

question: How can I use less energy at home?
poem:
Switch off the lights when you leave a room,
And unplug the chargers that idly consume;
Wear a warm sweater instead of more heat,
And wash clothes cooler to make savings complete.

question: Explain the Big Bang theory simply.
poem:
The Big Bang is the start of all that we know,
About thirteen point eight billion years ago;
Everything began very hot and small,
Then expanded and cooled to form stars and all.

question: Who was Einstein and why is he famous?
poem:
Albert Einstein was a physicist great,
Whose theory of relativity changed science's fate;
He showed that mass and energy are tied,
With E equals mc squared as his guide.

question: Are carrots really good for you?
poem:
Carrots contain a lot of vitamin A,
Which helps your eyes see in dim light each day;
They are full of fiber that helps you digest,
A crunchy snack that is one of the best.

question: What actually is a star?
poem:
A star is a ball of glowing gas,
That shines in the sky as the ages pass;
Our Sun is the star that is closest by,
The others are farther, so they look small in the sky.

question: What's the best way to learn a new language?
poem:
Practice a little every single day,
With apps, books, or songs that you like to play;
Speak with native speakers whenever you can,
And don't fear mistakes, they are part of the plan.

question: Which city is the capital of Italy?
poem:
The capital of Italy is Rome,
Where ancient ruins and churches make their home;
The Colosseum stands from a time long ago,
And the Vatican lies within it, as many know.

question: How does the stock market work?
poem:
The stock market is where shares are sold,
Small pieces of companies that people hold;
When a business grows, its shares may rise,
But prices can fall, so invest with wise eyes.

question: How does a submarine go underwater?
poem:
Submarines take in water to make them weigh more,
So they sink beneath waves toward the ocean floor;
To rise again, they push water out with air,
And float back up to the surface from there.

question: why do stars twinkle
poem:
Stars twinkle because of the air in between,
Its moving layers bend the light that is seen;
The light shifts and wobbles as it travels through,
So stars seem to sparkle in the night's deep blue.

question: capital of germany?
poem:
The capital of Germany is Berlin,
A city where history and art are woven in;
Its famous wall divided it in two,
Until it fell in nineteen eighty-nine, it's true.

question: I think I have the flu. What is it exactly?
poem:
The flu is caused by a virus that spreads,
And can send many people straight to their beds;
A yearly vaccine can help you stay well,
And washing your hands also helps, as doctors tell.

question: What does carbon footprint mean?
poem:
A carbon footprint counts the gases you make,
From the trips that you drive to the meals that you bake;
Flying less and saving power make it shrink,
More than most people might expect or think.

question: My houseplant keeps dying. How do I take care of it?
poem:
Give your plant water when the soil feels dry,
And find it a spot where the light comes by;
Too much water makes the roots slowly rot,
So drain any water left in the pot.

question: What are the Olympics?
poem:
The Olympics are games held every four years,
Where athletes compete to the crowd's loud cheers;
They began long ago in ancient Greece,
And now bring nations together in peace.

question: Why does an apple go brown after you cut it?
poem:
When you cut an apple, its cells break apart,
And oxygen in the air gets a start;
An enzyme reacts and turns the flesh brown,
Lemon juice slows it and keeps the color down.

question: How do hurricanes work?
poem:
A hurricane is a huge, spinning storm,
That forms over oceans where waters are warm;
Its winds can be strong enough to knock out power,
Blowing over one hundred nineteen kilometers an hour.

question: I have a job interview next week. How should I prepare?
poem:
Learn about the company before you go,
And think of examples of skills you can show;
Practice your answers out loud with a friend,
And bring a few questions to ask at the end.

question: Who built the Egyptian pyramids?
poem:
Egyptian workers, skilled and well fed,
Built the pyramids for kings who were dead;
They hauled huge stone blocks with ramps and with rope,
Guided by engineers with patience and hope.

question: Is it true that skin is an organ?
poem:
Your skin is the largest organ of all,
It wraps you from head to toe like a wall;
It keeps out germs and holds water in,
And helps you feel touch through the nerves in your skin.

question: Tell me about the Renaissance.
poem:
The Renaissance was a time of rebirth,
When learning and art showed their new worth;
It began in Italy six hundred years ago,
With artists like Leonardo putting on a show.

question: Why do we have to pay taxes?
poem:
Taxes are money we pay to the state,
To fund what we share, both small and great;
Like schools, roads, hospitals, and police,
Which help keep our towns running in peace.

question: How are clouds formed?
poem:
The Sun warms the water, which rises up high,
Then cools into droplets up in the sky;
These droplets gather on dust in the air,
And form the white clouds that float up there.

question: What makes an animal a mammal?
poem:
A mammal has hair or fur on its skin,
And feeds its young milk to help them begin;
Most give birth to live babies, not eggs, it is true,
Like dogs, whales, and humans, and bats and cows too.

question: Why do zebras have stripes?
poem:
Scientists think zebra stripes may keep biting flies away,
Those flies land on them less often, studies say;
The stripes might also help them stay cool in the heat,
Though the full answer is not yet complete.

question: How do bats see in the dark?
poem:
Bats send out squeaks as they fly through the night,
And listen for echoes instead of using sight;
The sounds bounce back from insects and walls,
So they know where things are as each echo calls.

question: Why do chameleons change their color?
poem:
Chameleons change color to show how they feel,
Or to warm up in sunlight, a clever deal;
Special cells in their skin reflect light in new ways,
And help them send signals on different days.

question: how long does an elephant live
poem:
Elephants in the wild can live sixty years or more,
The oldest females lead the herd they adore;
They remember water and paths for a long time,
And guide younger ones on the routes that they climb.

question: Why are owls active at night?
poem:
Owls have big eyes that see well in dim light,
So they hunt for their food in the dark of night;
Their soft feathers let them fly without sound,
To catch mice and voles moving on the ground.

question: How does a caterpillar turn into a butterfly?
poem:
A caterpillar eats leaves and grows fast and fat,
Then forms a chrysalis and rests inside that;
Its body is rebuilt in a total remake,
Then a butterfly emerges, with wings wide awake.

question: Why can't penguins fly?
poem:
Their wings became flippers, short, stiff, and strong,
For swimming through icy seas all day long;
Their heavy, solid bones help them dive deep below,
So they trade flying for speed where cold currents flow.

question: Do ants talk to each other?
poem:
Ants talk to each other with chemicals they leave,
Called pheromones, which their antennae receive;
They lay down a trail when they find something to eat,
So the others can follow it, step by step, with their feet.

question: Why do cows chew the same food twice?
poem:
Cows swallow their grass quickly and then rest,
Bringing it back up to chew it again is best;
Their stomach has four parts to break the grass down,
Letting them feed well in fields far from town.

question: How many hours a day do koalas sleep?
poem:
Koalas eat eucalyptus leaves all day long,
Though the leaves are tough and the smell is strong;
These leaves give little energy, so they sleep a lot,
Up to twenty hours a day in a shady spot.

question: How fast is a cheetah?
poem:
The cheetah is the fastest runner on land,
Its speed over short distances is truly grand;
It can reach about a hundred kilometers an hour,
But only for short bursts before losing its power.

question: Why do fireflies light up?
poem:
Fireflies make light through a chemical reaction,
And use it to signal and find mates by attraction;
Each kind flashes in its own pattern at night,
So partners can spot the right blinking light.

question: How do snakes move if they have no legs?
poem:
Snakes move by pushing their scales against the ground,
Bending their bodies in curves all around;
Their strong muscles ripple from head to tail,
So they glide along, leaving a winding trail.

question: Why do dolphins jump out of the water?
poem:
Dolphins leap from the water for many reasons, it seems,
To travel faster, to play, or to signal their teams;
Jumping can save energy when they swim at speed,
And may help them spot fish or birds where they feed.

question: How do trees get so tall?
poem:
Trees grow at their tips as they reach for the light,
Adding new cells that let them climb to great height;
Their trunks grow wider with a new ring each year,
Which shows their age when the wood is cut clear.

question: Why do some animals sleep all winter?
poem:
In winter, food is scarce and the weather is cold,
So some animals sleep as the seasons unfold;
Their heartbeat and breathing slow way down,
To save energy until spring comes to town.

question: Which bird is the biggest?
poem:
The ostrich is the largest bird you will find,
It cannot fly, but it leaves others behind;
It runs very fast on its two long legs,
And it lays the biggest of all birds' eggs.

question: How do spiders build their webs?
poem:
Spiders make silk inside their bodies to spin,
Pulling it out from their spinnerets to begin;
They weave sticky threads in a careful design,
To catch flying insects in a silky line.

question: Why do salmon swim up rivers?
poem:
Salmon swim upstream to the streams where they were born,
Fighting fast rivers, they leap, tired and worn;
They lay their eggs in the gravel of streams,
Starting a new generation, it seems.

question: How do plants drink water?
poem:
Plants pull up water through their roots below,
Into thin tubes in their stems where it can flow;
It rises as water evaporates from the leaves,
A steady pull that every plant achieves.

question: why are flamingos pink
poem:
Flamingos are pink because of the food that they eat,
Tiny shrimp and algae make the color complete;
These foods contain pigments that tint their feathers bright,
Without them, flamingos would look pale or white.

question: Do camels store water in their humps?
poem:
Camels store fat in their humps, not water inside,
Which gives them energy on a long desert ride;
They can go many days without having a drink,
Their bodies save water better than you might think.

question: Can you tell me what a coral reef is?
poem:
A coral reef grows from tiny animals in warm seas,
Their limestone skeletons pile up by degrees;
Reefs shelter fish, turtles, and many other kinds,
But warming oceans harm them, as research finds.

question: How do birds know where to go when they migrate?
poem:
Birds use the Sun and the stars as their guide,
And Earth's magnetic field helps them decide;
They also remember landmarks along the way,
Like rivers and mountains they pass each day.

question: Why do roosters crow in the morning?
poem:
Roosters have an inner clock that tells them the time,
So they crow at dawn as the sun starts to climb;
They also crow to mark their territory and space,
Letting other roosters know this is their place.

question: Do whales breathe air?
poem:
Whales are mammals, so they breathe air like you and me,
Coming up to the surface from deep in the sea;
They breathe through a blowhole on top of their head,
And can hold their breath long before rising instead.

question: Are mosquitoes attracted to some people more than others?
poem:
Only female mosquitoes bite, in need of a meal,
The protein in blood helps their eggs grow, for real;
They follow the carbon dioxide we exhale,
And the warmth of our bodies, a tempting trail.

question: Is it true that sunflowers follow the sun?
poem:
Young sunflowers turn to follow the sun through the day,
Facing east at sunrise, then west as it moves away;
As they grow older, the turning will stop,
And they face the east, with their heavy blooms on top.

question: What's the difference between a frog and a toad?
poem:
Frogs mostly have smooth skin that is moist and thin,
While toads have dry, bumpy, and warty skin;
Frogs leap far on their long, strong back legs,
While toads take short hops, and both lay eggs.

question: What are cats' whiskers for?
poem:
Cats use their whiskers to sense the space around,
They feel tiny movements in the air and on the ground;
Whiskers help them judge if a gap is wide enough,
And find their way at night when the path is rough.

question: How do earthworms help gardens?
poem:
Earthworms dig tunnels that let air and water in,
Where the roots of new plants can easily begin;
They eat dead leaves and leave behind their waste,
Which makes the soil richer, a plant's favorite taste.

question: Why do giraffes have such long necks?
poem:
Giraffes have long necks to reach leaves up high,
In tall acacia trees that other animals pass by;
Males also swing their necks when they fight,
Which may have helped long necks grow to their height.

question: How can jellyfish live without a brain?
poem:
Jellyfish have no brain, just a net of nerves inside,
That senses light and touch as they drift on the tide;
Their stinging tentacles catch the food they need,
So they can survive with simple bodies, indeed.

question: Why is grass green?
poem:
Grass is green because of chlorophyll inside,
A pigment that catches sunlight far and wide;
It absorbs red and blue light but not much green,
So green light bounces back, and that is what is seen.

question: How many times per second do hummingbirds flap their wings?
poem:
Hummingbirds beat their wings very fast to stay in place,
Tracing a figure eight in the air with grace;
Their wings beat dozens of times every second,
So they need lots of nectar, as scientists have reckoned.

question: Why do pine trees stay green in winter?
poem:
Evergreen trees keep their needles all year through,
Thin, waxy leaves that lose little water, it is true;
They shed and replace a few needles, never all,
So they stay green through winter, spring, summer, and fall.

question: How does an octopus change color?
poem:
An octopus changes color with cells in its skin,
That stretch or shrink with the pigments held within;
It can blend into rocks to hide from a threat,
Or flash bright warnings that predators won't forget.

question: Can horses sleep standing up?
poem:
Horses can doze standing, locking their legs in place,
So they can run quickly if danger shows its face;
But for deep sleep they must lie down on the ground,
For short periods, when they feel safe all around.

question: How do seeds spread to new places?
poem:
Seeds travel in many ways to find new ground,
Some float on the wind, spinning round and round;
Others ride in fur, or in birds that eat fruit,
Or drift down rivers to a new place to take root.

question: How does pollination work?
poem:
Pollination is when pollen moves from flower to flower,
Carried by bees, wind, or birds, it has great power;
It lets plants make the seeds and fruit they grow,
So new plants can sprout in the fields below.

question: Why is Mars red?
poem:
Mars looks red because of the dust on its ground,
Full of iron oxide, which is rust, all around;
Even its sky can look pink, as photos have shown,
A red, dusty world with a color of its own.

question: How many planets are there in the solar system?
poem:
There are eight planets that circle our Sun,
Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars, one by one;
Then Jupiter and Saturn, Uranus and Neptune too,
And Pluto now counts as a dwarf planet, it is true.

question: Why does Saturn have rings?
poem:
Saturn's rings are made of ice and rock,
In pieces from tiny grains to the size of a block;
They may come from moons or comets torn apart,
By Saturn's strong gravity, long ago at the start.

question: Comets: what are they made of?
poem:
A comet is a ball of ice, dust, and rock,
That circles the Sun on a long, slow clock;
When it nears the Sun, its ice turns to gas,
Making a glowing tail as it starts to pass.

question: Explain the Milky Way to a beginner.
poem:
The Milky Way is the galaxy where we live,
With billions of stars and the light that they give;
Our Sun is just one star in its spinning arms,
Far from its center, among its starry charms.

question: Why does the Moon change shape during the month?
poem:
The Moon has no light of its own, you know,
It reflects the Sun's light and gives off a glow;
As it orbits, we see different parts of its lit side,
From a thin crescent to a full Moon, bright and wide.

question: What happens during an eclipse?
poem:
An eclipse happens when the Sun, Moon, and Earth align,
And one blocks the light in a nearly perfect line;
When the Moon blocks the Sun, daylight fades away,
When Earth shades the Moon, it glows red and gray.

question: If the Sun is so bright, why is space dark?
poem:
Space has no air to scatter the light around,
So darkness surrounds us, with no blue to be found;
Light only shows where it hits something to see,
Like planets and moons, glowing bright and free.

question: How do astronauts sleep on the space station?
poem:
Astronauts sleep in bags strapped to a wall,
So they will not float off while they sleep at all;
Since the station sees many sunrises in a day,
They use eye masks to keep the light away.

question: How far is a light-year?
poem:
A light-year measures distance across space,
How far light travels in a year at its pace;
That is nearly ten trillion kilometers wide,
Used to measure the stars and the galaxies outside.

question: Why does the Sun always rise in the east?
poem:
The Earth spins from west to east each day,
So the Sun appears in the east, then moves away;
It seems to cross the sky and set in the west,
But it is Earth that turns, while the Sun stays at rest.

question: Explain what an atom is, simply.
poem:
An atom is the tiny building block of all,
Of everything around us, both big and small;
It has a nucleus of protons and neutrons inside,
With electrons moving around it, far and wide.

question: Why does ice float on water?
poem:
When water freezes, its molecules spread apart,
So ice is less dense than water from the start;
That lets ice float on lakes and on the sea,
Keeping the water below liquid for fish to swim free.

question: How does a battery work?
poem:
A battery holds chemicals that react inside,
Pushing electrons through a wire as their guide;
That flow of electrons powers your phone or your light,
Until the chemicals run down and the power is slight.

question: How would you explain electricity to a child?
poem:
Electricity is energy from charges that flow,
Moving through wires to make our lamps glow;
It can come from the wind, the sun, or a dam,
And power our homes, from the lights to the tram.

question: Why does the sea look blue?
poem:
The sea looks blue because water soaks up red light,
While blue light goes deeper and bounces back bright;
It also reflects the color of the sky above,
A view of deep blue that so many people love.

question: In biology class we talk about cells. What is a cell?
poem:
A cell is the smallest unit of life we know,
All living things are made of cells that grow;
Some creatures are just one cell, tiny and small,
While humans have trillions working for us all.

question: Why does metal feel colder than wood?
poem:
Metal and wood in one room share the same heat,
But metal pulls warmth from your skin, fast and neat;
It carries the heat from your fingers away,
While wood holds it back, so the warmth can stay.

question: Why do puddles disappear after the rain?
poem:
Evaporation is when a liquid turns into a gas,
Like puddles that vanish as sunny hours pass;
The water rises up into the air as vapor,
Which is why wet towels dry, and so does wet paper.

question: How does a thermometer measure temperature?
poem:
Old thermometers hold a liquid that expands with heat,
It climbs up a thin tube to a number, neat;
Digital ones use sensors that measure the change,
And show the temperature in a number range.

question: Why is the ozone layer important?
poem:
The ozone layer is a shield high in the sky,
That blocks harmful sunlight from passing by;
It absorbs much of the Sun's ultraviolet rays,
Protecting life on Earth through all of our days.

question: Why do we have time zones?
poem:
As Earth spins, the Sun reaches places at different times,
So noon in Paris is not noon in other climes;
The world is divided into zones, an hour apart,
So each place's clocks match the Sun from the start.

question: How are fossils made?
poem:
A fossil is the remains of life from long ago,
Like bones, shells, or footprints, preserved below;
Buried in layers of rock, they slowly turned to stone,
Teaching us about creatures we never could have known.

question: what were dinosaurs
poem:
Dinosaurs were reptiles that lived long before us,
Some tiny as chickens, some huge as a bus;
An asteroid ended most of their reign,
But birds are their cousins, still flying again.

question: Why do we sneeze?
poem:
You sneeze when something tickles inside your nose,
Like dust, pepper, or pollen as the wind blows;
Your body pushes air out in a powerful burst,
To clear away whatever is bothering you first.

question: Why do I get goosebumps?
poem:
Goosebumps appear when you feel cold or scared,
Tiny muscles pull your skin hairs up, raised and flared;
In furry animals, this traps warm air near the skin,
Or makes them look bigger when a fight might begin.

question: Do I really need to brush my teeth twice a day?
poem:
Brushing clears off plaque, a sticky film of germs,
That damages your teeth, as every dentist confirms;
Brush twice a day with a fluoride paste,
So cavities and gum problems go to waste.

question: What does the liver do?
poem:
Your liver cleans your blood of toxins every day,
And helps break down the things you eat along the way;
It stores energy and makes bile to digest fat,
A busy organ with many jobs, imagine that.

question: Which foods give us vitamins?
poem:
Vitamins help your body grow and stay strong,
They help every part of it work all day long;
You find them in fruits, vegetables, fish, and grains,
And a varied diet keeps up your body's gains.

question: What does it mean when food has a lot of calories?
poem:
Calories measure the energy that food can give,
The fuel your body burns to move and to live;
If you eat more than you use, it is stored as fat,
And if you use more, your body draws on that.

question: Why do we get a fever when we are sick?
poem:
A fever is how your body fights germs inside,
Raising its temperature so they find nowhere to hide;
Many germs grow slower when the body is warm,
And your defenses work faster to help you through the storm.

question: How do muscles get bigger?
poem:
When you lift or push, tiny fibers in muscles tear,
Then your body repairs them with protein and care;
They grow back a little thicker and strong,
If you rest and eat well as you go along.

question: Why do we blink?
poem:
We blink to keep our eyes wet and clean,
Spreading tears over them like a cleaning machine;
It also protects them from things flying near,
And gives them short rests to keep our vision clear.

question: How does taste work?
poem:
Taste buds on your tongue sense the flavors you eat,
Like salty, sour, bitter, umami, and sweet;
Your nose helps too, by smelling the food,
Which is why with a cold, flavors feel subdued.

question: Why do we dream?
poem:
Scientists still debate exactly why we dream,
Though several ideas are popular, it would seem;
Dreams may help us sort memories from the day,
And process our feelings in a nighttime way.

question: How does the immune system protect us?
poem:
Your immune system is a guard in your blood,
White cells attack germs like a fast-moving flood;
It makes antibodies that remember each foe,
So the next infection gets a quicker blow.

question: Why is sugar bad for teeth?
poem:
Bacteria in your mouth feed on the sugar you eat,
And make acids that attack your teeth, which is no treat;
These acids wear away enamel little by little,
Leaving teeth with holes and making them brittle.

question: What's in our blood?
poem:
Your blood is mostly plasma, a watery base,
That carries cells and nutrients to every place;
Red cells bring oxygen, white cells fight disease,
And platelets stop bleeding with remarkable ease.

question: How much water should I drink in a day?
poem:
Many adults need around two liters a day,
Though needs change with heat and exercise, they say;
Your food gives some water, like fruit and like stew,
So drink when you are thirsty, and check your pee's hue.

question: Which foods are high in protein?
poem:
Protein builds and repairs your muscles and skin,
Your hair, your nails, and the organs within;
You find it in beans, eggs, fish, and meat,
And nuts or dairy can make your meals complete.

question: Can antibiotics cure a virus?
poem:
Bacteria are living cells that can grow on their own,
But viruses cannot multiply alone;
Antibiotics can kill bacteria, it is true,
But they do not work against viruses like the flu.

question: How do solar panels work?
poem:
A solar panel turns sunlight into power,
Making electricity hour after hour;
Its cells are made of silicon that reacts to light,
Producing current while the Sun is shining bright.

question: How does a microwave heat up food?
poem:
A microwave sends waves that make water molecules spin,
Heating the food from the water within;
That motion makes heat, so your meal warms fast,
Though some spots stay cold, so stir it at last.

question: What is a satellite, and what do we use them for?
poem:
A satellite orbits a planet in space,
Like the Moon that circles Earth at its pace;
People also launch satellites that help us each day,
With weather, TV, and GPS along the way.

question: How does GPS know where I am?
poem:
GPS uses satellites high in the sky,
That send out signals as they pass by;
Your phone measures how long each signal takes to arrive,
And finds where you are as you walk or you drive.

question: Can you explain what a robot is?
poem:
A robot is a machine that can sense and act,
Following programs that tell it each step and fact;
Robots build cars, explore Mars, and clean floors,
Doing jobs that are dangerous or boring chores.

question: Why do helium balloons float?
poem:
A helium balloon floats because helium is light,
Lighter than air, so it rises in flight;
The heavier air around pushes it up high,
Until it pops or drifts away into the sky.

question: Explain friction with an everyday example.
poem:
Friction is the force that resists things that slide,
When two surfaces rub against each other side by side;
It helps your shoes grip and your bike's brakes stop,
But it also wears things out, from the bottom to the top.

question: Explain how a rocket gets off the ground.
poem:
A rocket burns fuel and pushes hot gas out the back,
Which pushes the rocket forward along its track;
As Newton's law says, each push has an equal reply,
So the gas going down sends the rocket up high.

question: Lemons are acidic, but what is an acid?
poem:
An acid is a substance that often tastes sour,
Like lemon juice or vinegar, with chemical power;
Acids have a pH below seven on the scale,
And strong ones can burn, so handle them with care without fail.

question: Why does iron rust?
poem:
Iron rusts when it meets water and air,
Oxygen joins it and leaves a red layer there;
This rust flakes away and weakens the metal,
So paint helps protect a bike or a kettle.

question: How does a tsunami start?
poem:
A tsunami begins when the sea floor shakes,
From earthquakes or landslides, the ocean wakes;
Giant waves race across the sea at great speed,
And flood the coast, so warnings are what people need.

question: Why are some people left-handed?
poem:
About one in ten people are left-handed, it is said,
A mix of genes and chance shapes how the hands are led;
Scientists think it begins before we are born,
And it is not something to fix or to scorn.

question: Explain the greenhouse effect simply.
poem:
Some gases in the air trap heat from the Sun,
Like a blanket around Earth when the day is done;
This natural effect keeps our planet warm,
But too much of these gases pushes beyond the norm.

question: How do glaciers form?
poem:
Glaciers form where more snow falls than melts away,
Year after year, piling up day after day;
The snow gets packed down into ice that is thick,
Which slowly flows downhill, never very quick.

question: Tell me about the Sahara desert.
poem:
The Sahara is the largest hot desert on Earth,
Spread across North Africa, vast in its girth;
It has sand dunes, rocks, and very little rain,
And temperatures that soar on its dry, open plain.

question: What's a tornado?
poem:
A tornado is a spinning column of air,
That reaches from a storm cloud down to the ground there;
Its winds can be the strongest on Earth, they say,
And it can tear apart houses in its way.

question: How does soap get rid of germs?
poem:
Soap molecules grab dirt and germs with one end,
While the other end holds water, a helpful blend;
They can break the oily coat that some viruses wear,
So rinsing washes them off and leaves your hands bare.

question: Why is the sky red at sunset?
poem:
At sunset, sunlight travels through more air,
So the blue light scatters away before it gets there;
The reds and the oranges are left to shine through,
Painting the evening sky with a warm, glowing hue.

question: What causes wind?
poem:
The Sun warms the ground unevenly each day,
Warm air rises up and cool air rushes its way;
That moving air is the wind on your face,
Flowing from high pressure to a low-pressure place.

question: Which city is Spain's capital?
poem:
The capital of Spain is Madrid,
Right in the middle, the country's center lid;
It has royal palaces and museums of art,
And lively squares in its historic heart.

question: what's the capital of the UK
poem:
London is the capital of the United Kingdom's land,
On the River Thames, historic and grand;
It has Big Ben, the Tower, and many a park,
And red double-decker buses from morning to dark.

question: Is New York the capital of the United States?
poem:
The capital of the United States is Washington, D.C.,
Not New York, though many think so, you see;
The White House stands there, where the president stays,
And Congress meets in the Capitol most days.

question: Is Cairo the capital of Egypt?
poem:
Cairo is the capital of Egypt, by the Nile,
A huge, busy city with an ancient style;
Near it, the pyramids of Giza stand tall,
The oldest of the world's wonders of all.

question: What's the capital of Russia?
poem:
Moscow is the capital of Russia, vast and cold,
With the Kremlin's red walls and domes of gold;
Red Square lies at its heart, wide and grand,
In the largest country by area on land.

question: Which city is the capital of China?
poem:
Beijing is the capital of China today,
Where the Forbidden City shows an emperor's way;
It is home to millions and a center of power,
With ancient temples and many a tower.

question: What's India's capital?
poem:
New Delhi is the capital of India, a city of power,
Where ministers meet and parliament works hour after hour;
It sits within Delhi, a city old and wide,
With markets and monuments on every side.

question: Mexico's capital is Mexico City, isn't it?
poem:
Mexico City is the capital, high in a valley's ground,
Built where the old Aztec capital once was found;
It is one of the largest cities on Earth,
Full of murals, markets, and cultural worth.

question: What's the capital of Argentina?
poem:
Buenos Aires is the capital of Argentina, so grand,
By a wide river estuary, on the coast of its land;
It is known for the tango, music, and dance,
And its cafes and streets full of style and romance.

question: Quick geography question: what's the capital of Kenya?
poem:
Nairobi is the capital of Kenya, in East Africa's land,
With a national park where wild animals stand;
Giraffes and lions roam close to the town,
With tall city buildings that look gently down.

question: What's the capital of Portugal?
poem:
Lisbon is the capital of Portugal by the sea,
Built on seven hills, as old as can be;
Its yellow trams climb up the steep streets,
And it is famous for custard tarts and sweet treats.

question: Athens is the capital of Greece, right?
poem:
Athens is the capital of Greece, ancient and bright,
Where the Parthenon stands on a rocky height;
It is often called the place where democracy grew,
And great thinkers like Socrates walked there too.

question: Is Rio de Janeiro the capital of Brazil?
poem:
Brazil's capital is not Rio, but Brasilia instead,
A city designed and built, as planners had said;
It opened in nineteen sixty, modern and new,
Shaped like an airplane when seen from a view.

question: What's the capital of South Korea?
poem:
Seoul is the capital of South Korea today,
Where old palaces and skyscrapers meet on the way;
It is famous for technology, food, and K-pop,
A busy city where the lights never stop.

question: Is Istanbul the capital of Turkey?
poem:
Many think Istanbul, but Ankara is the one,
Turkey's capital since nineteen twenty-three began its run;
Istanbul is larger and famous worldwide,
But the government sits on the Ankara side.

question: Is Casablanca the capital of Morocco?
poem:
Rabat is the capital of Morocco, by the sea,
Though Casablanca is larger, as many agree;
It has old city walls and gardens to see,
And a royal palace where the king may be.

question: What's the capital of Norway?
poem:
Oslo is the capital of Norway, by a fjord's blue,
Where the Nobel Peace Prize is handed out too;
It is green and surrounded by forest and sea,
With museums of Viking ships for all to see.

question: Which city is the capital of Sweden?
poem:
Stockholm is the capital of Sweden, built on isles,
Fourteen islands linked by bridges for miles;
Its old town has narrow streets of stone,
And its Nobel Prize ceremonies are widely known.

question: Does Switzerland have a capital?
poem:
Switzerland has no official capital by law,
But Bern serves as the federal city, without a flaw;
It is where the government and parliament meet,
With an old town of arcades along each street.

question: Brussels is the capital of Belgium, right?
poem:
Brussels is the capital of Belgium, it is true,
And home to many European Union offices too;
It is known for chocolate, waffles, and comics in print,
And a grand central square with a golden tint.

question: Which country is the biggest in the world?
poem:
Russia is the largest country by area of land,
Stretching across Europe and Asia, vast and grand;
It spans eleven time zones from west to east,
With forests, mountains, and tundra, to say the least.

question: What's the smallest country in the world?
poem:
Vatican City is the smallest country on Earth,
Inside Rome, it is small but rich in worth;
It is where the Pope lives and leads his church,
Covering less than half a square kilometer's search.

question: Which country has the largest population?
poem:
India has the most people of any land,
It passed China in twenty twenty-three, as planned;
Both have over one point four billion each,
More than any other country's reach.

question: How tall is the highest waterfall in the world?
poem:
Angel Falls in Venezuela is the highest of all,
From a flat-topped mountain comes its long fall;
It drops nearly a kilometer to the ground,
In a misty jungle where wild things are found.

question: Is the Sahara the biggest desert in the world?
poem:
Antarctica counts as the largest desert, it is true,
Because very little rain or snow falls there through;
A desert means dry, not always hot sand,
And the Sahara is the largest hot desert on land.

question: How deep is the deepest part of the ocean?
poem:
The deepest point is the Challenger Deep, far below,
In the Mariana Trench, where few have dared to go;
It is almost eleven kilometers down from the waves,
In total darkness, with strange creatures in its caves.

question: Which lake is the largest in the world?
poem:
The Caspian Sea is the largest lake you will find,
It is called a sea, but it is a lake of a kind;
It is salty and lies where Europe and Asia meet,
And five countries share its shores, a rare feat.

question: Where is the Amazon rainforest?
poem:
The Amazon rainforest grows in South America's land,
Mostly in Brazil, it is vast and grand;
It is the largest tropical rainforest on Earth,
And its rivers and trees are of immense worth.

question: Tell me about the Alps.
poem:
The Alps are a mountain range in Europe's heart,
Across France, Italy, Switzerland, and Austria they start;
Mont Blanc is their highest peak, white with snow,
Where skiers and climbers love to go.

question: Why was the Panama Canal built?
poem:
The Panama Canal was built to save time,
Cutting a path through the jungle and grime;
Ships cross from Atlantic to Pacific with ease,
Instead of sailing for weeks around stormy seas.

question: Where exactly is the equator?
poem:
The equator is an imaginary line around Earth's middle,
Dividing north and south, like a planet's riddle;
It is hot there all year, with sunshine strong,
And days and nights are about twelve hours long.

question: Why was Venice built on water?
poem:
Venice was built on islands in a lagoon long ago,
Where people fled invaders, safe from the foe;
They built on wooden posts driven into the ground,
And canals became streets where boats travel around.

question: Tell me about Kilimanjaro.
poem:
Kilimanjaro rises above the Tanzanian plain,
Africa's highest peak, with snow and with rain;
It is a sleeping volcano, quiet for ages,
And climbers reach its top in several stages.

question: Why is it called the Dead Sea?
poem:
The Dead Sea is a salty lake between two lands,
So salty that people float on it without using their hands;
Its shore is the lowest place on land on Earth,
And few living things can grow there since its birth.

question: Can you see the Great Barrier Reef from space?
poem:
The Great Barrier Reef lies off Australia's coast,
The largest coral reef system, which it can boast;
It can be seen from space, it stretches so far,
With fish of every color, shaped like a star.

question: What causes the northern lights?
poem:
The Northern Lights glow in the polar night sky,
When particles from the Sun come rushing by;
They hit the gases high in our air,
And paint green and pink curtains glowing there.

question: When did World War II end?
poem:
World War Two ended in nineteen forty-five,
After years of fighting that few could survive;
In Europe it ended in May of that year,
And in Asia by September, the peace became clear.

question: When did World War I start?
poem:
World War One began in nineteen fourteen,
The deadliest war the world had then seen;
It started after an archduke was killed in Sarajevo one day,
And ended in nineteen eighteen, with millions passed away.

question: Who was the first US president?
poem:
George Washington was the very first to lead,
The new United States in its time of need;
He served for two terms and then chose to leave,
A peaceful handover others would later achieve.

question: What happened during the French Revolution?
poem:
The French Revolution began in seventeen eighty-nine,
When people rose up against the king's design;
They stormed the Bastille and demanded rights for all,
And the old monarchy came to its fall.

question: Who was Julius Caesar and how did he die?
poem:
Julius Caesar was a Roman general long ago,
Who conquered Gaul and put on a great show;
He took power in Rome as a leader of great might,
But senators killed him, fearing his height.

question: How big was the Roman Empire?
poem:
The Roman Empire ruled lands far and wide,
From Britain to Egypt, with Rome as its pride;
It built roads, aqueducts, and laws that still stand,
And for centuries it shaped Europe's land.

question: Tell me about Cleopatra.
poem:
Cleopatra was the last queen of ancient Egypt's throne,
Clever and powerful, she ruled as her own;
She spoke many languages and made alliances with Rome,
Trying to protect her kingdom and her home.

question: What was the Cold War?
poem:
The Cold War was a long rivalry after World War Two,
Between the United States and the Soviet Union, it is true;
They raced to build weapons and explore space,
But never fought each other directly, face to face.

question: When did the Berlin Wall come down?
poem:
The Berlin Wall fell in nineteen eighty-nine,
In November, people crossed the dividing line;
Families reunited after years apart,
And Germany united again, a brand new start.

question: What did Christopher Columbus do?
poem:
Christopher Columbus was a sailor from Genoa's shore,
Who crossed the Atlantic in fourteen ninety-two to explore;
He reached the Americas, though he thought it was Asia's land,
And his voyages brought great change and harm, we understand.

question: Why is Joan of Arc so famous in France?
poem:
Joan of Arc was a French peasant girl, brave and bold,
Who led French troops in battle, as the stories have told;
She helped lift the siege of Orleans long ago,
And became a saint whose story many know.

question: Why is Martin Luther King Jr. important?
poem:
Martin Luther King Junior fought for civil rights,
Leading peaceful marches through days and through nights;
He gave the famous speech that began with a dream,
Of equality and justice as a shared theme.

question: What did Nelson Mandela fight for?
poem:
Nelson Mandela fought against apartheid's unfair laws,
And spent twenty-seven years in prison for his cause;
When freed, he was elected South Africa's head,
And chose peace and forgiveness to lead instead.

question: What was the Industrial Revolution?
poem:
The Industrial Revolution started in Britain long ago,
When machines and factories made production grow;
Steam engines powered mills, trains, and ships,
And changed how people worked and made their trips.

question: What did Gandhi do for India?
poem:
Mahatma Gandhi led India toward being free,
With peaceful protest and nonviolence as his key;
He marched to the sea to make salt in defiance,
Inspiring the world with his calm reliance.

question: How many people were on the Titanic?
poem:
The Titanic was a huge ship that set sail with pride,
In nineteen twelve, with over two thousand inside;
It hit an iceberg on its very first trip,
And sank in the cold Atlantic, a tragic ship.

question: Who invented the printing press?
poem:
Johannes Gutenberg built a printing press with care,
Around fourteen forty, with movable type to share;
Books could be printed quickly and spread far and wide,
So knowledge reached people on every side.

question: Who were the Vikings?
poem:
The Vikings were seafarers from Scandinavia's land,
Who sailed in long ships with oars in their hand;
They raided and traded on many a shore,
And even reached North America to explore.

question: Explain what the Silk Road was.
poem:
The Silk Road was a network of trading routes long ago,
Linking China to Europe, where goods would flow;
Merchants carried silk, spices, and tea,
And ideas traveled too, from sea to sea.

question: Was Leonardo da Vinci only a painter?
poem:
Leonardo da Vinci was a genius of Italy's past,
A painter, inventor, and thinker whose fame would last;
He painted the Mona Lisa and the Last Supper too,
And sketched flying machines long before they were true.

question: Why is Shakespeare so famous?
poem:
William Shakespeare was an English writer of plays,
Still performed on stages in modern days;
He wrote Hamlet, Macbeth, and many more,
And added new words that English speakers adore.

question: What did Isaac Newton discover?
poem:
Isaac Newton was an English scientist of great fame,
Who explained how gravity works, with laws that bear his name;
He studied light and colors and how objects move,
And his ideas gave science a strong groove.

question: What is Charles Darwin known for?
poem:
Charles Darwin sailed the world on a ship long ago,
And studied how living things change as they grow;
He explained evolution by natural selection,
Where the best suited survive, in nature's direction.

question: Why did Galileo get in trouble?
poem:
Galileo Galilei looked at the sky through a telescope he made,
And saw Jupiter's moons, which his findings displayed;
He supported the idea that Earth moves around the Sun,
Which caused him trouble with the church, but science won.

question: How many people have walked on the Moon?
poem:
The Apollo program was NASA's mission to the Moon,
In the sixties and seventies, sending astronauts soon;
Six missions landed, with twelve people who walked there,
And brought back rocks to study with care.

question: Tell me about the painter Frida Kahlo.
poem:
Frida Kahlo was a Mexican painter, bold and bright,
Who painted herself in colors full of light;
After a bus accident left her in pain,
She turned her suffering into art again and again.

question: Was Mozart really a child genius?
poem:
Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was a composer of renown,
A child prodigy who played in every court and town;
He wrote symphonies and operas, filled with delight,
And died young, but his music still shines bright.

question: Tell me about Beethoven.
poem:
Beethoven was a German composer of great might,
Who kept writing music when he lost his hearing outright;
His Ninth Symphony ends with a choir's loud song,
And his works have inspired musicians all along.

question: What did Victor Hugo write?
poem:
Victor Hugo was a French writer of great renown,
Who wrote about Paris and the poor of the town;
Les Miserables and Notre-Dame de Paris are his best known,
And he fought for justice in the works he has shown.

question: Tell me about the writer Albert Camus.
poem:
Albert Camus was a French writer born in Algeria's land,
Who wrote The Stranger and The Plague, books in high demand;
He asked how to live in a world without clear reason,
And won the Nobel Prize for writing in nineteen fifty-seven's season.

question: Why is Simone de Beauvoir important?
poem:
Simone de Beauvoir was a French thinker and writer,
Whose ideas on women's freedom made the future brighter;
She wrote The Second Sex, a famous book of her day,
That shaped feminism in a powerful way.

question: Who painted The Starry Night?
poem:
Vincent van Gogh painted The Starry Night,
With swirling skies and stars that glow bright;
He painted it in France in eighteen eighty-nine,
Using bold brushstrokes and a twisting line.

question: Explain impressionism to me.
poem:
Impressionism was an art movement born in France,
Where painters caught light and moments at a glance;
Monet and Renoir painted outdoors with quick strokes,
Showing scenes of nature and everyday folks.

question: Why is the Louvre so famous?
poem:
The Louvre is a famous museum in Paris, France,
Once a royal palace, now art's grand expanse;
It holds the Mona Lisa and ancient statues too,
And a glass pyramid welcomes visitors through.

question: What's the story of the Statue of Liberty?
poem:
The Statue of Liberty stands in New York's harbor bay,
A gift from France to the United States one day;
She holds a torch up high as a symbol of the free,
Welcoming ships that arrived from across the sea.

question: Why was the Taj Mahal built?
poem:
The Taj Mahal is a white marble tomb in India's land,
Built by an emperor for his wife, beautiful and grand;
It took many years and thousands of workers to make,
And it shines at sunrise beside a garden and a lake.

question: Tell me about Machu Picchu.
poem:
Machu Picchu is an Inca city in the Andes, it is true,
Built on a mountain in Peru with a breathtaking view;
Its stone walls fit together without any glue,
And thousands of visitors climb up to walk through.

question: What was the Colosseum used for?
poem:
The Colosseum is an ancient arena in Rome,
Where crowds once gathered as in a great stone home;
Gladiators fought there in contests of old,
And its ruins still stand, impressive and bold.

question: Who built Stonehenge and why?
poem:
Stonehenge is a ring of huge stones in England's land,
Raised about five thousand years ago by hand;
No one knows exactly why it was made,
But it lines up with the Sun as the seasons fade.

question: Why do Americans celebrate Thanksgiving?
poem:
Thanksgiving in the United States gives thanks for the year,
With family dinners and turkey to share and to cheer;
It recalls a harvest feast from sixteen twenty-one,
And is held each November when the harvest is done.

question: How is Chinese New Year celebrated?
poem:
Chinese New Year starts with the new Moon's glow,
In late January or February, as calendars show;
Families share dumplings and red envelopes bright,
With dragon dances and fireworks lighting the night.

question: What happens during Ramadan?
poem:
Ramadan is a holy month in the Islamic year,
When many Muslims fast from dawn until the night is near;
They eat before sunrise and after the sun goes down,
And celebrate its end with Eid in every town.

question: How do people celebrate Diwali?
poem:
Diwali is the festival of lights in India and beyond,
Celebrated by Hindus, Sikhs, and Jains, of which they are fond;
People light small lamps and share sweets with friends,
As light over darkness is the message it sends.

question: Why do the French celebrate July 14th?
poem:
Bastille Day is France's national day each year,
On July fourteenth, with parades and fireworks to cheer;
It marks the storming of the Bastille long ago,
In seventeen eighty-nine, as French people know.

question: What do the Olympic rings mean?
poem:
The Olympic flag has five rings joined on white,
Blue, yellow, black, green, and red, linked tight;
They stand for the continents taking part in the games,
United in sport with all their different names.

question: When was the United Nations created?
poem:
The United Nations was founded in nineteen forty-five,
To keep peace among nations and help people thrive;
Nearly every country is a member today,
And they meet to solve problems in a peaceful way.

question: How does the European Union work?
poem:
The European Union is a group of countries that agree,
To trade and work together, with many borders free;
Many use the euro as their money each day,
And make shared laws in a cooperative way.

question: Why are there so many different languages?
poem:
Languages changed as groups of people spread apart,
Each developing its own words and its own art;
Over thousands of years, these changes grew,
So now there are thousands of languages, it is true.

question: How many languages are there in the world?
poem:
There are about seven thousand languages spoken today,
Though many are small and may fade away;
Mandarin, Spanish, English, and Hindi are widely known,
But each language carries a culture of its own.

question: What's the most spoken language in the world?
poem:
English has the most speakers when learners are counted too,
But Mandarin has the most native speakers, it is true;
Spanish and Hindi are also spoken by many,
And each one has speakers numbering plenty.

question: Where does English come from?
poem:
English grew from tongues that Germanic tribes brought,
To Britain long ago, as historians have taught;
Later, Norse, Latin, and French added many new terms,
Making English a mix, as its history confirms.

question: How many letters are in the English alphabet?
poem:
An alphabet is a set of letters for each sound,
Used to write words in languages all around;
The English one has twenty-six letters in a row,
From A to Z, as every student will know.

question: What are Egyptian hieroglyphs?
poem:
Hieroglyphs were the writing of ancient Egypt's land,
With pictures and symbols carved and painted by hand;
The Rosetta Stone helped scholars understand,
What those mysterious signs meant and planned.

question: What's the oldest city in the world?
poem:
No one knows for sure which city came first of all,
But Jericho and Damascus are strong names to recall;
People have lived in them for thousands of years,
Through wars, floods, and changing frontiers.

question: Why do people call Paris the City of Light?
poem:
Paris is called the City of Light for good reason,
It was a center of ideas in the Enlightenment season;
It was also among the first to light its streets at night,
Which made the whole city glow with light.

question: Tell me about the Mediterranean Sea.
poem:
The Mediterranean Sea lies between three lands,
Europe, Africa, and Asia, with sunny sands;
Ancient Greeks, Romans, and Egyptians sailed there,
Trading goods and ideas with great care.

question: Tell me about the Arctic.
poem:
The Arctic is the icy region around the North Pole,
Where sea ice covers the ocean as a whole;
Polar bears hunt seals on the frozen sea,
But the ice is shrinking as warm years come to be.

question: What is Antarctica like?
poem:
Antarctica is the frozen continent at the South Pole,
Covered in ice sheets thick as a whole;
No country owns it, by a treaty agreed,
And scientists study its climate there indeed.

question: Why is it called the Ring of Fire?
poem:
The Ring of Fire circles the Pacific Ocean wide,
Where many volcanoes and earthquakes reside;
Tectonic plates meet and move along its line,
So eruptions and quakes are a common sign.

question: Why does Japan get so many earthquakes?
poem:
Japan sits where several tectonic plates meet,
They grind and push in a slow, steady beat;
When stress builds up and the rocks suddenly slip,
The ground shakes hard, from the coast to the tip.

question: Tell me about the Nile.
poem:
The Nile flows north through Africa to the sea,
One of the longest rivers that there can be;
Ancient Egyptians farmed along its banks each year,
When floods brought rich soil, and harvests were near.

question: Where does the Mississippi River flow?
poem:
The Mississippi is a great river in the United States,
It flows south to the Gulf past cities and their gates;
It drains water from much of the land,
And steamboats once traveled its waters so grand.

question: What are the Himalayas?
poem:
The Himalayas are the highest mountains on Earth,
Formed when India pushed into Asia since its birth;
Mount Everest is there, the tallest peak of all,
And the range keeps rising, though the change is small.

question: How much water do I need to cook rice?
poem:
Rinse the rice, then add two cups of water for each one,
Bring it to a boil, then lower the heat until done;
Cover the pot and let it simmer fifteen minutes or so,
Then rest it for five, and fluff it before you go.

question: How long should I cook pasta?
poem:
Boil a big pot of water and add some salt,
Then add the pasta and stir so it does not halt;
Cook it for the time that the package will say,
Then drain it and add your sauce right away.

question: How do you make pancakes?
poem:
Mix flour, milk, eggs, and a little sugar too,
Whisk until the batter is smooth all the way through;
Pour small circles in a hot, buttered pan,
Flip when bubbles appear, as fast as you can.

question: How can I make a simple salad?
poem:
Wash some fresh lettuce and tear it in a bowl,
Add tomatoes and cucumber to round out the whole;
Mix oil, vinegar, and salt for a dressing,
Toss it all together, a healthy blessing.

question: How do I make an omelette?
poem:
Beat two or three eggs with a pinch of salt,
Pour them in a hot pan with butter, without fault;
Add cheese or herbs as the eggs start to set,
Then fold it in half, the best one yet.

question: How do I bake my own bread?
poem:
Mix flour, water, yeast, and a little salt,
Knead the dough until it is smooth, with no fault;
Let it rise until it doubles in size,
Then bake it until it is golden, a tasty prize.

question: How do I make a homemade soup?
poem:
Chop onions, carrots, and celery to start,
Cook them in oil until they soften apart;
Add broth, vegetables, and herbs to the pot,
Simmer until tender and serve it hot.

question: How can I keep bread from going stale?
poem:
Store your bread in a cool, dry place,
In a bag or a bread box, a closed space;
For longer, slice it and freeze it with care,
Then toast a slice whenever you want it there.

question: How long do leftovers last in the fridge?
poem:
Most cooked leftovers last three or four days,
If kept in the fridge in covered trays;
Cool them quickly before you put them away,
And throw them out if they smell bad or turn gray.

question: Why should I eat more vegetables?
poem:
Vegetables give vitamins, minerals, and fiber too,
They help your heart and your gut work well for you;
They are low in calories and full of good things,
And a colorful plate gives the health that it brings.

question: Is it bad to skip breakfast?
poem:
Breakfast can give you energy to start the day,
And help you focus at work, at school, or at play;
But people differ, and what you eat matters most,
More than the time you sit down to your toast.

question: How do I make coffee without a machine?
poem:
Heat fresh water until it is almost boiling hot,
Add ground coffee to a filter or a pot;
Pour the water slowly and let it drip through,
Then add milk or sugar if that suits you.

question: What does a balanced diet look like?
poem:
A balanced diet has fruits and vegetables each day,
With whole grains and protein along the way;
It limits sugar, salt, and heavily processed food,
And water each day keeps you in a good mood.

question: I always put things off until the last minute. How do I stop procrastinating?
poem:
Break big tasks into small steps you can do,
And start with just five minutes to get through;
Put your phone in a drawer, out of sight,
And reward yourself after work done right.

question: How can I get up earlier in the morning?
poem:
Go to bed earlier, a little each night,
And open the curtains to let in the light;
Put your alarm across the room so you rise,
And keep the same schedule to train your eyes.

question: How should I organize my day?
poem:
Write down your tasks and choose the most important one,
Plan your day so the hardest work gets done;
Use a calendar to block time for each task,
And leave short breaks, as your focus will ask.

question: Any tips to be more productive at work?
poem:
Focus on one task at a time, not three,
Turn off notifications so your mind is free;
Work in short blocks with small breaks in between,
And tidy your desk so your workspace is clean.

question: What's the best way to study for an exam?
poem:
Start studying early instead of the night before,
Review your notes and practice questions galore;
Test yourself often and explain things out loud,
Then sleep well the night before, calm and proud.

question: How can I remember things better?
poem:
Sleep well each night so memories can settle in,
And review what you learn so it stays within;
Link new ideas to things you already know,
And test yourself often to help them grow.

question: How do I give a good presentation?
poem:
Know your main message and keep it clear,
Practice out loud so your words come near;
Use simple slides with few words on each one,
And speak slowly, looking at people, till you are done.

question: I'm scared of public speaking. How can I get over it?
poem:
Prepare well and practice your talk many times,
Like learning a song with its rhythm and rhymes;
Breathe slowly and remember the crowd wants you to win,
And focus on your message as you begin.

question: How do I write a good CV?
poem:
Keep your CV short, one or two pages at most,
List your experience and the skills you can boast;
Use clear headings and verbs that show what you did,
And check for mistakes so no errors are hid.

question: How should I ask my boss for a raise?
poem:
Gather proof of your results and your work,
Show the value you bring and every extra perk;
Check what similar jobs are paid in your field,
Then ask calmly and clearly, and be ready to yield.

question: How can I become a better listener?
poem:
Look at the person and give them your mind,
Put down your phone and be patient and kind;
Do not interrupt, let them finish each thought,
Then repeat what you heard to check what you caught.

question: One of my coworkers is really difficult. What should I do?
poem:
Stay calm and polite when tension is high,
And try to understand the reason why;
Talk to them privately about what went wrong,
And ask a manager for help if it lasts too long.

question: How can I spend less on groceries?
poem:
Make a list before you go to the store,
And stick to it so you do not buy more;
Compare the prices per kilo you see,
And cook at home, which costs less than takeaway fee.

question: How do I make a budget?
poem:
A budget is a plan for the money you get,
It lists what you spend so you avoid debt;
You track your income and your costs each week,
And save a part first, as the experts speak.

question: How does a bank account work?
poem:
A bank account keeps your money safe in a bank,
You can pay with a card instead of cash, to be frank;
A savings account may pay interest as you go,
A small reward that helps your money grow.

question: What does interest on a loan mean?
poem:
Interest is the price you pay to borrow money,
It adds to what you owe, which is not very funny;
The higher the rate, the more you will pay,
So compare loans carefully before you sign away.

question: Are credit cards a bad idea?
poem:
A credit card lets you buy now and pay later,
But unpaid balances make your debt much greater;
If you pay the full amount each month in a timely way,
You avoid the interest and keep your record okay.

question: What's the difference between saving and investing?
poem:
Saving keeps money safe for needs close at hand,
In a bank account where it can steadily stand;
Investing buys assets that may grow over time,
But their value can fall as well as climb.

question: Should I have an emergency fund?
poem:
An emergency fund is money set aside,
For surprise costs, so you have a safety ride;
Like a broken car or a job that you lose,
It gives you time to plan and freedom to choose.

question: How does a mortgage work?
poem:
A mortgage is a loan to buy a house or a flat,
You repay it over many years, and that is that;
The home secures the loan, so if payments stop,
The bank can take the home, a painful drop.
